mappings.note: Volume of the largest cone inscribed in a cube. Only the cone's own volume is wanted, so nothing is added or subtracted (not C-7.2-LO-3) and no material changes shape (not C-7.3-LO-3). Single-solid mensuration has no LO in this frame, so the competency is the finest true code.

Turns entirely on realising the cut exposes two NEW flat faces, so 2x(2pi r^2 + pi r^2), not 4pi r^2. That is choosing which component areas count before adding - C-7.1-LO-4 - rather than computing a combined solid's area (C-7.2-LO-2).
Plain cone volume from base area and height, one solid. No combination and no recasting, so neither C-7.2-LO-3 nor C-7.3-LO-3.
Scaling a single sphere's volume by the cube of the radius factor. Not a combination and nothing is recast; the competency is the only code that covers one basic solid.
A sphere is melted and re-formed as cubes and smaller spheres; the whole method is equating volumes across a change of shape. That is C-7.3-LO-3, not C-7.2-LO-3, because nothing is joined together.
Two separate solids compared by their curved surface formulas; they are never combined, so C-7.2-LO-2 (surface area of a combined solid) does not apply.
Surface area of a single cube from the perimeter of one face. One solid, no join, no recast.
Ratio of lateral surfaces of two separate cylinders. Comparison, not combination, so not C-7.2-LO-2.

Volume of a spherical shell is outer sphere MINUS inner sphere - a composite volume obtained by subtraction, which is C-7.2-LO-3. C-7.1-LO-4 was rejected because the subtraction is of volumes, not areas.
Ratio of volumes of two separate cylinders of equal height. Single-solid formula applied twice, not a combination.
Ratio of volumes of two separate cones of equal radius. Same reason as the cylinder ratio item: comparison, not combination.
Sphere melted and drawn into a wire - the canonical recast, sphere volume equated to a long cylinder. Not C-7.2-LO-3, which needs two solids standing together.
Cylinder with a cone of the same base and height removed: volume of a combination by subtraction. Nothing is melted, so not C-7.3-LO-3.

The whole point is that the two flat faces vanish inside the join, so only the curved pieces are added. Selecting which component surfaces survive is C-7.1-LO-4; the arithmetic afterwards is trivial, so C-7.2-LO-2 would overstate it.
Pure recognition of how an enclosed sphere sits in a cylinder - the sphere's diameter is the cylinder's diameter. No area or volume is computed at all, so only the component-recognition outcome fits.
States the governing principle of recasting itself: volume is unaltered when a solid is converted to another shape. It is the defining idea of C-7.3-LO-3 rather than any combination outcome.
Cuboid moulded into a sphere - one solid becomes another of a different shape, volume equated.
One cylinder melted into twelve spheres. Recast with a count, so C-7.3-LO-3 and not C-7.2-LO-3.

Asks what a plane parallel to the base cuts from a cone, with 'frustum' as the trap distractor. It is frustum analysis but determines neither curved surface area nor volume, so C-7.3-LO-2 would be wrong; the competency is the honest level.
Volume ratio of two spheres converted to a surface-area ratio via r^3 then r^2. Two separate spheres, no combination and no recast.

The one genuine frustum item in the chapter: works the frustum relation l = sqrt((R-r)^2 + h^2) to get h. C-7.3-LO-3 is wrong (nothing is recast); the fit to LO-2 is imperfect because LO-2 names only curved surface area and volume, and this asks for the height.
Total surface area of one cylinder from the standard formula. Single solid, so no combination outcome applies.
Slant height of a single cone from r and h. Basic-solid relation, not a composite and not a frustum (the frustum form has (R-r) in it).
Single sphere scaled by radius; same content as the Section A item 4 but posed as a very-short answer. One solid, no join, no recast.
Melted sphere re-formed as cubes and smaller spheres; solved by equating the two halves' volumes across a change of shape.
